title: Genomic analysis of early case samples from the 2025 Marburg virus outbreak in Ethiopia - Nature

analysis.time: The outbreak was first reported on 14 November 2025, with the outbreak concluding by December 2025. The genomic analysis was conducted in 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The outbreak occurred in Ethiopia, specifically in Jinka, Ari Zone, South Ethiopia Regional State. The affected population included 4,006 individuals investigated and 155 suspected cases, with 14 confirmed cases and 9 deaths.
analysis.event: Ethiopia reported its first outbreak of Marburg virus disease in November 2025, with genomic analysis of seven early case samples revealing the outbreak lineage belonged to the MARV.A.1 clade. The outbreak was confirmed through reverse transcription PCR (RT–PCR) at the Ethiopian Public Health Institute (EPHI).
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The outbreak resulted in 14 confirmed cases and 9 deaths, with a case fatality rate of 64%. The genomic analysis indicated limited within-outbreak diversity, suggesting a single zoonotic spillover event followed by human-to-human transmission. The risk of further spread was highlighted through the identification of potential mutations in key viral genes.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The Ethiopian government implemented a comprehensive emergency response within 48 hours of confirming MVD, including contact tracing, isolation, expanded diagnostic capacity, community engagement, and the deployment of antiviral drugs and vaccines. The findings emphasize the importance of genomic surveillance for outbreak detection and response.

analysis.brief_en: In November 2025, Ethiopia reported its first outbreak of Marburg virus disease, with a case fatality rate of 64%. Genomic analysis of seven early case samples revealed that the outbreak lineage belonged to the MARV.A.1 clade, closely related to historical human cases and bat-derived sequences. The outbreak was confirmed through reverse transcription PCR (RT–PCR) at the Ethiopian Public Health Institute (EPHI), and a comprehensive emergency response was rapidly implemented, including contact tracing, isolation, and expanded diagnostic capacity. By December 2025, 14 confirmed cases and 9 deaths were recorded, with most patients being young male adults. The analysis showed limited within-outbreak diversity, suggesting a single zoonotic spillover event followed by human-to-human transmission. The Ethiopian lineage was closely related to the human MARV isolate JN408064, which originated from a Dutch patient infected in 2008 after visiting Python Cave in Uganda. The findings highlight the importance of genomic surveillance for outbreak detection, response, and preparedness, as well as the need for expanded longitudinal studies to distinguish between different transmission scenarios.

title: No licensed vaccine or drug exists as Marburg virus outbreaks multiply across Africa - Bioengineer.org

analysis.time: The article was published on 2026-10-28. The event date is 14 November 2025, when Ethiopia confirmed its first-ever Marburg outbreak. The review was published on 9 August 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The outbreaks have occurred across Africa, including Ethiopia, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Angola, Equatorial Guinea, Tanzania, Rwanda, and others. The affected population includes humans and animals, with transmission occurring through body fluids and contaminated objects.
analysis.event: Marburg virus outbreaks have been reported across Africa, with Ethiopia confirming its first-ever outbreak on 14 November 2025. The article states that no licensed vaccine or drug exists for the disease, and the review highlights the challenges in understanding the disease's epidemiology and treatment options.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Since the virus was first identified in 1967, more than 600 cases have been recorded globally, with an average case fatality rate of around 50 percent. Case fatality rates vary widely, from 24 to 88 percent, depending on factors such as outbreak size, access to supportive care, and surveillance completeness. The disease is a severe and frequently fatal zoonotic haemorrhagic fever.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The review synthesises current knowledge about the disease and its countermeasures, but no licensed vaccine or drug exists. The article notes that the lack of a vaccine or treatment has hindered efforts to control outbreaks. The review excludes preprints and unpublished data, and the case fatality rate is difficult to interpret as a measure of care quality due to reporting bias.

analysis.brief_en: The article published on 2026-10-28 by Bioengineer.org highlights the ongoing Marburg virus outbreaks across Africa, emphasizing the absence of a licensed vaccine or drug. Ethiopia confirmed its first-ever Marburg outbreak on 14 November 2025, and the virus has been responsible for multiple outbreaks in sub-Saharan Africa since its initial identification in 1967. The review published in Discover Viruses on 9 August 2026, led by Amit Bansal and colleagues, synthesizes current knowledge about the disease's epidemiology, virology, and treatment options, drawing on peer-reviewed literature up to 13 February 2026. The review notes that Marburg virus disease is a severe and frequently fatal zoonotic haemorrhagic fever, with case fatality rates ranging from 24 to 88 percent. These rates are influenced by factors such as outbreak size, access to supportive care, and surveillance completeness. The article also mentions that the virus causes clinically indistinguishable illness from Ravn virus, both members of the Filoviridae family. Despite the severity of the disease, no licensed vaccine or drug exists, and the lack of robust clinical trials has limited the development of effective treatments. The review underscores the challenges in interpreting case fatality rates due to reporting bias and limited sample sizes, particularly in small outbreaks where only a few cases are detected. The article further notes that the virus spreads through body fluids and contaminated objects, and outbreaks have been associated with healthcare practices and burial rituals. The absence of a vaccine or treatment remains a critical issue in managing Marburg virus outbreaks.

source_language_evidence.event: 2025年埃塞俄比亚马尔堡病毒暴发早期病例样本的基因组学分析。
source_language_evidence.scale_impact_and_risk: - 基因组多样性与选择压力:埃塞俄比亚谱系共鉴定出148个谱系定义替换,其中110个位于编码序列(CDS)内,包括28个非同义替换和82个同义替换;38个位于基因间隔区。GP基因是主要分歧热点,包含13个固定非同义替换,如受体结合域的Q205K、粘蛋白样结构域的11个替换(K222N、D250N、A284T、S291P、P295L、N310D、G317D、H336R、T343I、K465E、S485P)以及膜融合区的N501H。VP35含1个非同义替换(S193A);L基因含9个非同义替换(A115V、I359V、I1643T、Q1787R、P1796S、D1806N、R2091K、K2156Q、V2278A),为第二高值;NP和VP基因多样性极低。所有基因的dN/dS<1,提示强烈的纯化选择约束。
source_language_evidence.brief_en: 2025年埃塞俄比亚马尔堡病毒暴发早期病例样本的基因组学分析 《Nature Microbiology》:Genomic analysis of early case samples from the 2025 Marburg virus outbreak in Ethiopia 【字体: 大 中 小 】 时间:2026年10月30日 来源:Nature Microbiology 18.7 为了促进科学的传播,生物通采集了这篇文章 订阅BioHot点这里解锁原文链接推送! “畅读会员”点此登录查看原文链接 Brief Communication Open access 2025年11月,埃塞俄比亚报告了该国首次马尔堡病毒病(Marburg virus disease,MVD)暴发,病例致死率为64%。研究人员报告了对来自7例早期病例的7个近完整马尔堡病毒(Marburg virus,MARV)基因组的分析。此次暴发株属于MARV.A.1分支,该分支与历史人类病例及蝙蝠来源的基因组密切相关。这7个基因组之间的高核苷酸同一性表明,在一次人畜共患溢出事件后发生了人与人之间的传播。这些发现凸显了基因组监测在疫情检测、应对和防范中的重要性。 马尔堡病毒病(Marburg virus disease,MVD)是一种由马尔堡病毒(Marburg virus,MARV)引起的高致死性人畜共患感染,病例致死率可达23%至90%。2025年11月,埃塞俄比亚报告了该国首次MVD暴发,病例致死率为64%,亟需通过基因组学手段明确病毒来源、传播动态及进化特征,以支持疫情应对。论文发表于《自然·微生物学》(Nature Microbiology),研究人员对7例早期病例的7个近完整病毒基因组进行了测序和整合分析,为疫情监测和干预策略提供了关键依据。 索取T 细胞活化抗体最新资料 领 取 研究人员在埃塞俄比亚公共卫生研究所(EPHI)对7例经逆转录PCR(RT–PCR)确认的病例样本进行了全基因组测序,并获得覆盖度≥30×、可置信共识序列覆盖>90%的基因组。这些基因组与全球公开的103条正马尔堡病毒(Orthomarburgvirus)全基因组序列整合,构成包含110条序列、跨越13个国家(1967至2025年)的数据集,用以开展系统发育和进化分析。主要技术方法包括:使用Illumina RNA Prep with Enrichment(Viral Surveillance Panel 2)进行文库制备,并在NovaSeq X Plus和MiSeq平台测序;原始读段经fastp质控和修剪、HOSTILE去除人类宿主序列后,以BWA-MEM比对至MARV参考基因组(NC_001608.3),利用iVar完成变异检测和一致性序列组装;随后使用MAFFT进行多序列比对,IQ-TREE构建。

title: Genomes from Ethiopia’s first Marburg outbreak reveal post-spillover human transmission - Bioengineer.org

analysis.time: In November 2025, Ethiopia reported its first outbreak of Marburg virus disease. The study was published on October 29, 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: Ethiopia, specifically the Integrated Pathogen Genomics and Bioinformatics Facility for Surveillance and Research in Addis Ababa, with a focus on the affected population during the outbreak.
analysis.event: Genomic analysis of seven near-complete Marburg virus genomes from the first outbreak in Ethiopia revealed post-spillover human-to-human transmission. The study was conducted by researchers from the Ethiopian Public Health Institute (EPHI), the Federal Ministry of Health, and international collaborators.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The outbreak had a case fatality rate of 64%. Seven genomes were successfully sequenced, with 14 specimens initially RT–PCR-positive for Marburg virus. The findings highlight the importance of genomic surveillance for outbreak response and preparedness.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study was approved by the EPHI Institutional Review Board. All samples were anonymized, and the research was conducted under biosafety protocols. The genomic analysis was part of the EpiGen-Ethiopia project, which aims to build scalable genomic surveillance capacity in Ethiopia.

analysis.brief_en: In November 2025, Ethiopia experienced its first outbreak of Marburg virus disease, with a reported case fatality rate of 64%. A genomic analysis, published on October 29, 2026, revealed that the outbreak lineage belonged to the MARV.A.1 clade, indicating post-spillover human-to-human transmission. The study, conducted by researchers from the Ethiopian Public Health Institute (EPHI), the Federal Ministry of Health, and international collaborators, involved sequencing seven near-complete Marburg virus genomes from early cases. These genomes were obtained from patients suspected of having viral haemorrhagic fever, presenting with symptoms like high fever and muscle pain. The analysis was part of the EpiGen-Ethiopia project, which focuses on building genomic surveillance capacity for emerging infectious diseases. The findings emphasize the value of genomic surveillance in outbreak detection and response, as well as the importance of biosafety protocols and ethical practices in handling infectious samples.
analysis.summary_en: In November 2025, Ethiopia experienced its first outbreak of Marburg virus disease, with a reported case fatality rate of 64%. A genomic analysis, published on October 29, 2026, revealed that the outbreak lineage belonged to the MARV.A.1 clade, indicating post-spillover human-to-human transmission. The study, conducted by researchers from the Ethiopian Public Health Institute (EPHI), the Federal Ministry of Health, and international collaborators, involved sequencing seven near-complete Marburg virus genomes from early cases. These genomes were obtained from patients suspected of having viral haemorrhagic fever, presenting with symptoms like high fever and muscle pain. The analysis was part of the EpiGen-Ethiopia project, which focuses on building genomic surveillance capacity for emerging infectious diseases. The findings emphasize the value of genomic surveillance in outbreak detection and response, as well as the importance of biosafety protocols and ethical practices in handling infectious samples.

title: IAVI announces award from BARDA to transfer manufacturing of viral hemorrhagic fever vaccine candidates - IAVI

analysis.time: Affordable, accessible vaccines & antibodies We are a global nonprofit biomedical research organization that develops vaccines and antibodies for HIV, tuberculosis, and emerging infectious diseases.
analysis.location_and_population: IAVI, a global nonprofit biomedical research organization, is developing vaccines for Marburg virus and other emerging infectious diseases.
analysis.event: IAVI has received an award from BARDA to transfer manufacturing of Marburg virus vaccine candidates.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: IAVI's Marburg vaccine candidate has shown high protective efficacy in preclinical trials. The vaccine is based on a recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus (rVSV) vector.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: IAVI is conducting Phase 2 clinical trials for the Marburg vaccine candidate, which is the first to enter this phase. The vaccine is also being prioritized for development by the WHO during the ongoing epidemic.

analysis.brief_en: IAVI, a global nonprofit biomedical research organization, has received an award from BARDA to transfer manufacturing of Marburg virus vaccine candidates. The vaccine, based on a recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus (rVSV) vector, has shown high protective efficacy in preclinical trials and is now in Phase 2 clinical trials. The WHO has prioritized this vaccine during the ongoing epidemic.
analysis.summary_en: IAVI, a global nonprofit biomedical research organization, has received an award from BARDA to transfer manufacturing of Marburg virus vaccine candidates. The vaccine, based on a recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus (rVSV) vector, has shown high protective efficacy in preclinical trials and is now in Phase 2 clinical trials. The WHO has prioritized this vaccine during the ongoing epidemic.
